# Running the nf-core/rnaseq pipeline v3.27.0

**This is the first thing you do today.** Before analysing anyone else's count
matrix, you produce one yourself, so that the table the notebooks start from is not
a black box.

Processing a whole dataset needs more compute than we have in a classroom, so you run
two human airway smooth muscle samples from the dexamethasone experiment, one treated
and one untreated, sub-sampled to 50,000 reads each. The reference is a 5 Mb slice of
chromosome 19 rather than the whole genome, for the same reason.

<div class="important">
  <strong>⭐ What this run is, and what it is not.</strong> Two files of 50,000 reads
  against 5 Mb of one chromosome are enough to watch the pipeline work and to read its
  quality report. They are far too few to draw biology from, so <strong>you will not
  analyse your own output</strong>. Once you have seen how reads become counts, the
  notebooks pick up from the full count matrices, made with this same pipeline, which are
  already in <code>data/</code>. If you go looking for your pipeline output in notebook
  01, you will not find it - that is expected.
</div>

We use pipeline release [v3.27.0](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.27.0) with the
`star_salmon` aligner: STAR for alignment and Salmon for quantification. Human
genes have introns, so the aligner has to be splice-aware. (For bacteria this is
unnecessary, which is why the advanced *S. aureus* track uses the `prokaryotic`
profile and Bowtie2 instead.)

**To process the data, run the following command:**

```bash
bash 00_pipeline/00_nfcore_rnaseq_processing_human.sh
```

That script runs:

```bash
nextflow run 'https://github.com/nf-core/rnaseq' \
    -r 3.27.0 \
    -profile docker \
    --aligner star_salmon \
    --input  'data/seq_files_subsampled/PRJNA229998_GSE52778_human/samplesheet_PRJNA229998_subsampled_2samples.csv' \
    --outdir 'results/human/nfcore_rnaseq_processing_downsampled' \
    --fasta  'data/genome_files/human/chr19_GRCh38_48115444-53115443.fna.gz' \
    --gtf    'data/genome_files/human/chr19_GRCh38_48115444-53115443.gtf.gz' \
    --gtf_group_features 'gene_id' \
    --featurecounts_feature_type 'exon' \
    -c 00_pipeline/custom.config \
    -c 00_pipeline/human_demo.config
```

**What the arguments mean:**

-   `-r`: which release of the pipeline to use
-   `-profile`: run the tools in `docker` containers
-   `--aligner`: `star_salmon`, i.e. STAR for alignment and Salmon for quantification
-   `--input`: the sample sheet, listing each sample and its two fastq files
-   `--outdir`: where results go (the folder is created for you)
-   `--fasta`: the genome sequence, here the chromosome 19 slice
-   `--gtf`: the matching annotation
-   `-c`: two small config files. One caps CPUs and memory so the run fits in a
    Codespace; the other sets a handful of switches that cannot be passed on the
    command line.

It takes about **20 to 25 minutes**.

<div class="warning">
  <strong>⚠️ Free the disk space afterwards.</strong> A Codespace does not have room for
  two pipeline runs. This one fills roughly half the disk, almost all of it intermediate
  files that you do not need once the run has finished. When it completes, run:

```bash
rm -rf work .nextflow*
```

  This keeps everything in <code>results/</code> and throws away the rest. The one thing
  you give up is <code>-resume</code>: Nextflow re-uses the <code>work</code> directory to
  skip steps it has already done, so after deleting it a re-run starts from the beginning.
  That is a fair trade here, because the run is short.
</div>

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note:</strong> If you finish early and want to see how a bacterial dataset
  differs, run the cleanup above first, then
  <code>bash 00_pipeline/00_nfcore_rnaseq_processing_saureus.sh</code>. It uses two
  <em>S. aureus</em> USA-100 samples and the <code>prokaryotic</code> profile, and takes
  about 10 minutes. Without the cleanup it will run out of disk part-way through.
</div>

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Remember:</strong> You can also set parameters through the nf-core website instead of typing them.
  Go to the [pipeline page](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.27.0), press **Launch version 3.27.0**, fill in the form,
  and it generates a config file you can pass to Nextflow.
</div>

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note:</strong> The counts the notebooks use were made with this same pipeline on the full
  datasets: the human samples against the whole GRCh38 genome, and all three time points for both
  <em>S. aureus</em> strains with Bowtie2. The scripts for those runs are in
  <code>00_pipeline/</code> if you want to see the exact commands.
</div>

## Structure of the output directory

Results are written to `results/human/nfcore_rnaseq_processing_downsampled`.
The top level looks like this:

```
.
├── fastqc
├── fq_lint
├── multiqc
├── pipeline_info
├── star_salmon
└── trimgalore
```

What each folder holds:

-   **`star_salmon`** - the important one. Alignments (`.bam`), per-sample Salmon quantification, and the merged count matrices for the whole run. `salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv` and `salmon.merged.gene.SummarizedExperiment.rds` are what an analysis like the next chapter starts from.
-   **`fastqc`** - read quality reports, before (`raw`) and after (`trim`) trimming.
-   **`fq_lint`** - format checks on the fastq files.
-   **`multiqc`** - everything above gathered into one report. Start here.
-   **`pipeline_info`** - what ran, for how long, with which software versions. This is your reproducibility record.
-   **`trimgalore`** - adapter and quality trimming reports.

A closer look inside `star_salmon`, for one sample:

```
star_salmon
├── N052611_dexamethasone/              # per-sample Salmon output
│   ├── quant.sf                        #   transcript-level estimates
│   └── quant.genes.sf                  #   gene-level estimates
├── N052611_dexamethasone.sorted.bam
├── N052611_dexamethasone.sorted.bam.bai
├── log/                                # STAR alignment logs
├── samtools_stats/                     # alignment summaries per sample
├── deseq2_qc/                          # a quick PCA and sample distances
├── salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv       # merged counts, genes x samples
├── salmon.merged.gene_tpm.tsv          # merged TPM
├── salmon.merged.gene.SummarizedExperiment.rds
└── salmon.merged.tx2gene.tsv           # transcript to gene mapping
```

## Reading the MultiQC report

MultiQC collects the quality metrics from every step into a single page, so you
can compare all samples side by side instead of opening reports one at a time.

<div class="warning">
  <strong>⚠️ Your own mapping rate will look terrible, and that is correct.</strong>
  Around 1 to 2 per cent of reads map uniquely, and most are reported as "unmapped: too
  short". The reads come from the whole transcriptome, but the reference is 5 Mb of one
  chromosome, so almost nothing has anywhere to map. A QC number means nothing until you
  know what was mapped against what.
</div>

Because of that, we will look at the report from the full human dataset,
processed before the course:
[MultiQC report, human ASM](https://github.com/biosustain/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/blob/main/data/data-02-Homo_sapiens/hasapiens/multiqc/data-02-Homo_sapiens_multiqc_report.html).
On GitHub, click **Download raw file** and open it in your browser. In a
Codespace, right-click the file and choose **Open Preview**.

Things worth looking at:

- The general statistics table at the top, one row per sample
- FastQC metrics: read quality, GC content, adapter content, duplication, before and after trimming
- How many reads aligned, per sample
- The PCA and sample-distance heatmap from DESeq2
- Software versions, at the very end

Spend a few minutes going through it. Use the menu on the left to move around.
We will talk about what you found afterwards.

:::boxy
Sample names tell you the donor and the treatment, for example
`N052611_dexamethasone` is donor N052611 treated with dexamethasone, and
`N052611_untreated` is the matching untreated sample from the same donor.
:::
